newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: BANKING SECTOR PULLING OUT OF CRISIS - IBCA.
newsitem.headline: BANKING SECTOR PULLING OUT OF CRISIS - IBCA.

text.p: Lithuania's banking sector is on the road to recovery after being rocked by a crisis in late 1995, rating agency IBCA said on Wednesday.

"Banks' annual reports have indicated some improvement in loan portfolio quaility over the past twelve months and internal risk management controls have improved," the agency said in a report on the Lithuanian banking sector.
"The results of the banking sector for the first nine months of 1996 indicated a gradual recovery from the period of the worst problems in 1995," the report added.
IBCA said that the main trends in the sector included an increase in assets and deposits and a fall in interest rates.
"Total assets grew by 25 percent (in the first nine months of 1996), which resulted mainly from an increase in the banks' Treasury bill portfolios and their interbank operations," the report said.
"Deposits increased by 16 percent, reflecting some return to confidence in the sector," it added.
IBCA also said that interest spreads dropped from a high of five to 14 percent to four to eight percent, while average interest rates fell to ten percent from 30 percent.
The report said that loans grew by five percent in the first nine months of 1996 but noted that they decreased in "real" terms because of inflation.

IBCA traced the roots of the 1995 crisis to the difficulties faced by an economy in transition, coupled with inexperienced bank managers, which led to a "dramatic worsening in the quality of some banks' loan portolios."
This resulted in the insolvency and bankruptcy of around 15 of the 28 banks operating in the country at the end of 1994, IBCA said.

"To a certain extent these problems can be ascribed to the weakness of the regulation and supervision carried out by the central bank in the early 1990s when these were relatively new functions," the report said.
But it added that it was encouraged by the decisive steps taken by the central bank to tighten rules and improve supervision.

"The Lithuanian authorities implemented...regulatory changes during 1996 and early 1997 aimed at tightening prudential controls, bringing them into line with the best practices in developed countries," IBCA said.
Improvements cited in the report include increased transparency of banks' financial statements and the introduction of International Accounting Standards (IAS).
The IBCA report was prepared in adavnce of the agency's plans to assign ratings to a number of Lithuanian banks this year, an IBCA official in London told Reuters.
